claim: Chronic restraint stress (RS) application for 2 hours daily for 2 weeks increases immobility in the tail suspension test (TST) in wild-type mice.
source: The behavioral analyses demonstrated that the RS group had increased immobility in both the TST (Figure 1B, Videos 1 and 2; p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests (TST) comparing control and RS groups, with statistical significance (p < 0.001), and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Chronic restraint stress (RS) application for 2 hours daily for 2 weeks increases immobility in the forced swimming test (FST) in wild-type mice.
source: The behavioral analyses demonstrated that the RS group had increased immobility in both the TST (Figure 1B, Videos 1 and 2; p < 0.001) and FST (Figure 1C, Videos 3 and 4; p < 0.001) compared with the CTR group.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests (FST) comparing control and RS groups, with statistical significance (p < 0.001), and is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The increase in immobility due to chronic restraint stress is not due to reduction of general locomotor activity.
source: The increase in immobility is unlikely to be due to the reduction of general locomotor activity, because there was no significant difference in travel distance measured by the OFT between the CTR and the RS groups (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; p = 0.52).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the open-field test (OFT) showing no significant difference in travel distance between control and RS groups (p = 0.52), as shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Chronic restraint stress for 2 weeks does not significantly alter the time spent in the center zone in the open-field test.
source: Although animals receiving chronic stress has sometimes shown the decreased time spent in the center (Kim and Han, 2006; Choi et al., 2014; Simard et al., 2018; Song et al., 2020), our results showed no significant difference in the time between the CTR and the RS groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; p = 0.09).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the open-field test showing no significant difference in center zone time between control and RS groups (p = 0.09), as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B. The claim also references prior studies showing different results.

claim: The increase in immobility in the TST and FST has been considered as despair-like behaviors similar to phenotypes observed in patients with depression.
source: The increase in immobility in the TST and FST has been considered as a despair-like behaviors (Wang et al., 2017; Planchez et al., 2019), which is similar to one of phenotypes observed in patients with depression.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Wang et al., 2017; Planchez et al., 2019) that have characterized increased immobility in TST and FST as despair-like behaviors.

claim: Chronic restraint stress application for 2 weeks enhances c-Fos expression in the deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN).
source: The expression of c-Fos in the percentage of all DAPI positive cells for the RS group was significantly enhanced (Figure 1F; p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing significantly enhanced c-Fos expression in the DCN of the RS group compared to control (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Chronic restraint stress application for 2 weeks significantly enhances c-Fos expression in the dentate nucleus (DN) of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: The expression of c-Fos in the percentage of all DAPI positive cells for the RS group was significantly enhanced (Figure 1F; p < 0.001), particularly in the DN and in the IPN (Figure 1G; DN: p < 0.001; IPN: p = 0.036)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing significantly enhanced c-Fos expression in the DN of the RS group compared to control (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Chronic restraint stress application for 2 weeks significantly enhances c-Fos expression in the interposed nucleus (IPN) of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: The expression of c-Fos in the percentage of all DAPI positive cells for the RS group was significantly enhanced (Figure 1F; p < 0.001), particularly in the DN and in the IPN (Figure 1G; DN: p < 0.001; IPN: p = 0.036)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing significantly enhanced c-Fos expression in the IPN of the RS group compared to control (p = 0.036), as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Chronic restraint stress application for 2 weeks does not substantially change c-Fos level in the fastigial nucleus (FN) of the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: In contrast, there was no substantial change in c-Fos level in the FN (Figure 1G; p = 0.74).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing no significant change in c-Fos expression in the FN of the RS group compared to control (p = 0.74), as shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Most c-Fos-positive cells in the DCN after chronic restraint stress are NeuN-positive neurons.
source: Most of the c-Fos-positive cells had an overlap with NeuN (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-staining analysis showing overlap between c-Fos and NeuN, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: c-Fos-positive cells in the DCN after chronic restraint stress are not GAD67-positive inhibitory neurons.
source: Most of the c-Fos-positive cells had an overlap with NeuN (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), but not with GAD67 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-staining analysis showing no overlap between c-Fos and GAD67, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: c-Fos-positive cells in the DCN after chronic restraint stress are GFAP-negative, indicating they are not glial cells.
source: As previously reported (Groteklaes et al., 2020), clear signals of GFAP, a marker of glial cells, were not detected in the DCN, and consequently, cFos-positive cells in the DCN were GFAP negative (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-staining analysis showing c-Fos-positive cells are GFAP-negative, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, and is consistent with a prior study (Groteklaes et al., 2020).

claim: Cells in the DCN activated by chronic restraint stress are glutamatergic neurons.
source: These results indicate that cells in the DCN activated by RS are glutamatergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing c-Fos-positive cells are NeuN-positive but not GAD67-positive or GFAP-positive, indicating they are excitatory neurons.

claim: c-Fos expression in the DN is significantly enhanced after 3 days of restraint stress application.
source: The c-Fos expression in the RS group was significantly enhanced compared with the CTR group even by 3 days of RS application, and was maintained at elevated level after 7- or 10-day RS application (Figure 1H; 3, 7, or 10 days: p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing significantly enhanced c-Fos expression in the DN after 3 days of RS (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: c-Fos expression in the DN is maintained at elevated levels after 7 or 10 days of restraint stress application.
source: The c-Fos expression in the RS group was significantly enhanced compared with the CTR group even by 3 days of RS application, and was maintained at elevated level after 7- or 10-day RS application (Figure 1H; 3, 7, or 10 days: p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing significantly enhanced c-Fos expression in the DN after 7 or 10 days of RS (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Longer restraint stress duration induces c-Fos expression in more DCN neurons.
source: although the calculation of percentage increase in c-Fos-positive cells over CTR group suggests that longer RS induced c-Fos expression in more DCN neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E; p = 0.003).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing a significant increase in the percentage of c-Fos-positive cells with longer RS duration (p = 0.003), as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: DCN neurons in the DN are activated at the early stage of chronic stress.
source: Thus, the DCN neurons in the DN were already activated at the early stage of chronic stress, suggesting that the DCN neuron activity is involved in stressful situations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing c-Fos expression is enhanced in the DN after 3 days of RS, indicating early activation.

claim: Crus I of the cerebellum is involved in higher brain functions such as emotion and sociability.
source: Among these cortical regions, crus I is well recognized for its involvement in higher brain functions, such as emotion and sociability (Ferrari et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2020; Tsai et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Ferrari et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2020; Tsai et al., 2018; Turner et al., 2007) that have demonstrated the involvement of crus I in emotion and sociability.

claim: Changes in functional connectivity were observed in crus I of patients with depression.
source: Even though the topographic organization of stress-associated responses in the cerebellum is complex, changes in functional connectivity were observed in crus I of patients with depression (Alalade et al., 2011; Depping et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Alalade et al., 2011; Depping et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2012) that have observed changes in functional connectivity in crus I of patients with depression.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of Purkinje cells (PCs) in crus I using hM3Dq (Gq) and CNO increases spontaneous firing of PCs in vitro.
source: Cell-attached recordings from Gq-expressing PCs in cerebellar slices showed increased spontaneous firing after CNO application (10 μM) compared with the baseline, whereas the PCs in the uninfected cerebellum demonstrated no effects of CNO application (Figure 2B; Gq-PCs: t(8) = 3.7, p = 0.003; uninfected PCs: t(14) = 0.19, p = 0.85).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell-attached recordings showing increased PC firing after CNO application in Gq-expressing PCs (p = 0.003), as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Intraperitoneal administration of CNO into mice expressing Gq in PCs results in increased c-Fos level in Gq-expressing PCs in crus I in vivo.
source: The increase in activity was also confirmed in vivo by immunohistochemical analysis of c-Fos, which showed that intraperitoneal administration of CNO into mice expressing Gq in PCs resulted in an increased c-Fos level in Gq-expressing PCs in crus I (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing increased c-Fos expression in Gq-expressing PCs after CNO administration, as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Chronic chemogenetic activation of crus I PCs during restraint stress reduces c-Fos expression in the DN.
source: In addition, when we used this chemogenetic tool for enhancing crus I PC activity by the daily injection of CNO for the 2 weeks prior to RS application (Figure 2D), c-Fos expression in the DN was reduced compared with when only RS was applied (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing reduced c-Fos expression in the DN after chronic chemogenetic activation of crus I PCs during RS, as shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Chronic chemogenetic activation of crus I PCs during restraint stress restores c-Fos expression in the DN to control levels.
source: Quantified data showed that c-Fos-positive cells in the DN after chronically enhancing the activity of crus I PCs during RS were significantly decreased and the level was equivalent to the control (Figure 2F; RS – Gq-CNO: t(11) = –4.25, p < 0.001; CTR – Gq-CNO: t(11) = –0.43, p = 0.67).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from immunohistochemical analysis showing c-Fos expression in the DN after chronic chemogenetic activation of crus I PCs during RS is significantly decreased compared to RS alone (p < 0.001) and is equivalent to control (p = 0.67), as shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CNO administration itself without stereotaxic AAV injection does not affect RS-dependent depression-like behaviors in the TST.
source: The RS-dependent behavioral changes were not affected by either administration of saline or CNO, as seen by the significantly longer immobile times than the CTR group, but the similar immobile times to the RS group, in both the TST and FST (Figure 2G and H; CTR – RS-Sal, TST: t(41) = 3.91, p < 0.001, FST: t(41) = 3.88, p < 0.001; CTR – RS-CNO, TST: t(42) = 4.01, p < 0.001, FST: t(42) = 3.52, p < 0.001; RS – RS-Sal, TST: t(41) = –0.29, p = 0.77, FST: t(41) = 0.12, p = 0.9; RS – RS-CNO, TST: t(42) = –0.24, p = 0.81, FST: t(42) = –0.29, p = 0.78).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing CNO administration without AAV injection does not significantly alter immobility time in the TST compared to RS alone (p = 0.81), as shown in Figure 2G.

claim: CNO administration itself without stereotaxic AAV injection does not affect RS-dependent depression-like behaviors in the FST.
source: The RS-dependent behavioral changes were not affected by either administration of saline or CNO, as seen by the significantly longer immobile times than the CTR group, but the similar immobile times to the RS group, in both the TST and FST (Figure 2G and H; CTR – RS-Sal, TST: t(41) = 3.91, p < 0.001, FST: t(41) = 3.88, p < 0.001; CTR – RS-CNO, TST: t(42) = 4.01, p < 0.001, FST: t(42) = 3.52, p < 0.001; RS – RS-Sal, TST: t(41) = –0.29, p = 0.77, FST: t(41) = 0.12, p = 0.9; RS – RS-CNO, TST: t(42) = –0.24, p = 0.81, FST: t(42) = –0.29, p = 0.78).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing CNO administration without AAV injection does not significantly alter immobility time in the FST compared to RS alone (p = 0.78), as shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Saline or CNO administration itself does not affect travel distance in the open-field test.
source: The travel distance measured by the OFT was also unaffected by the saline or CNO administration (Figure 2I; CTR – RS-Sal, t(41) = –0.68, p = 0.5; CTR – RS-CNO, t(42) = –0.46, p = 0.65; RS – RS-Sal, t(41) = –0.11, p = 0.91; RS – RS-CNO, t(42) = 0.12, p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the open-field test showing no significant difference in travel distance with saline or CNO administration, as shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Intraperitoneal administration of saline or CNO itself has no effects on RS-dependent depression-like behaviors.
source: These results confirm that the intraperitoneal administration of saline or CNO itself has no effects on the RS-dependent depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing no significant differences in behavioral tests (TST, FST, OFT) between RS groups with saline or CNO administration and RS alone.

claim: CNO administration to PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I shortens immobile time in the TST compared to the RS group.
source: In contrast, CNO administration to the PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I, referred to as the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group, but not saline administration (RS-Gq-PC-Sal group), shortened the immobile time in both the TST and FST (Figure 2J and K). As unilateral and bilateral excitation of crus I PCs resulted in similar trends in all the TST, FST, and OFT, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–1F, combined results are presented in the main figures (Figure 2J–L). Even though there was considerable individual variability in all groups, the average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group was significantly shorter than that of the RS group, but was indistinguishable to the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(51) = –2.18, p = 0.03, FST: t(51) = –2.75, p = 0.007; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(64) = 1.66, p = 0.1, FST: t(64) = –0.12, p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing CNO administration to mice expressing Gq in crus I PCs significantly shortens immobility time in the TST compared to RS alone (p = 0.03), as shown in Figure 2J.

claim: CNO administration to PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I shortens immobile time in the FST compared to the RS group.
source: In contrast, CNO administration to the PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I, referred to as the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group, but not saline administration (RS-Gq-PC-Sal group), shortened the immobile time in both the TST and FST (Figure 2J and K). As unilateral and bilateral excitation of crus I PCs resulted in similar trends in all the TST, FST, and OFT, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–1F, combined results are presented in the main figures (Figure 2J–L). Even though there was considerable individual variability in all groups, the average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group was significantly shorter than that of the RS group, but was indistinguishable to the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(51) = –2.18, p = 0.03, FST: t(51) = –2.75, p = 0.007; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(64) = 1.66, p = 0.1, FST: t(64) = –0.12, p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing CNO administration to mice expressing Gq in crus I PCs significantly shortens immobility time in the FST compared to RS alone (p = 0.007), as shown in Figure 2K.

claim: CNO administration to PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I results in immobile time in the TST that is indistinguishable from the control group.
source: Even though there was considerable individual variability in all groups, the average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group was significantly shorter than that of the RS group, but was indistinguishable to the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(51) = –2.18, p = 0.03, FST: t(51) = –2.75, p = 0.007; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(64) = 1.66, p = 0.1, FST: t(64) = –0.12, p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing CNO administration to mice expressing Gq in crus I PCs results in immobility time in the TST that is not significantly different from control (p = 0.1), as shown in Figure 2J.

claim: CNO administration to PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I results in immobile time in the FST that is indistinguishable from the control group.
source: Even though there was considerable individual variability in all groups, the average immobile time in the RS-Gq-PC-CNO group was significantly shorter than that of the RS group, but was indistinguishable to the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(51) = –2.18, p = 0.03, FST: t(51) = –2.75, p = 0.007; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-CNO, TST: t(64) = 1.66, p = 0.1, FST: t(64) = –0.12, p = 0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing CNO administration to mice expressing Gq in crus I PCs results in immobility time in the FST that is not significantly different from control (p = 0.91), as shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Saline administration to PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I does not shorten immobile time in the TST compared to the RS group.
source: The immobile time in RS-Gq-PC-Sal group was conversely indistinguishable to that of the RS group, but was significantly longer than the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(51) = –0.57, p = 0.57, FST: t(51) = –0.33, p = 0.74; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(64) = 3.45, p < 0.001, FST: t(64) = 2.55, p = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing saline administration to mice expressing Gq in crus I PCs does not significantly alter immobility time in the TST compared to RS alone (p = 0.57), as shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Saline administration to PCP2-Cre mice expressing Gq specifically in the PCs of crus I does not shorten immobile time in the FST compared to the RS group.
source: The immobile time in RS-Gq-PC-Sal group was conversely indistinguishable to that of the RS group, but was significantly longer than the CTR group (Figure 2J and K; RS – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(51) = –0.57, p = 0.57, FST: t(51) = –0.33, p = 0.74; CTR – RS-Gq-PC-Sal, TST: t(64) = 3.45, p < 0.001, FST: t(64) = 2.55, p = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing saline administration to mice expressing Gq in crus I PCs does not significantly alter immobility time in the FST compared to RS alone (p = 0.74), as shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The open-field test showed unchanged distance movement in all four groups (CTR, RS, RS-Gq-PC-Sal, RS-Gq-PC-CNO).
source: The OFT showed unchanged distance movement in all four groups (Figure 2L; F(3,115) = 0.33, p = 0.33), ruling out the possibility that the different immobile times arose from altered general locomotor activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the open-field test showing no significant difference in distance movement among the four groups (p = 0.33), as shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The increase in activity of DCN neurons driven by chronic mild stress promotes the generation of depression-like behaviors.
source: These results in behavior, together with the c-Fos data, suggest that the increase in activity of DCN neurons driven by the chronic mild stress promotes the generation of depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing increased c-Fos expression in DCN neurons after chronic stress and behavioral data showing that chemogenetic manipulation of crus I PCs, which inhibit DCN neurons, reduces depression-like behaviors.

claim: Excitatory manipulation of crus I PC activity during RS application suppresses the generation of depression-like behaviors by inhibiting the activity of DCN neurons in the DN.
source: Consequently, the excitatory manipulation of crus I PC activity during RS application suppressed the generation of depression-like behaviors by inhibiting the activity of DCN neurons in the DN.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that chemogenetic excitation of crus I PCs reduces c-Fos expression in the DN and reduces depression-like behaviors.

claim: Cerebellar neuronal activity contributes to the stress-dependent development of depression-like behaviors.
source: We hence conclude that cerebellar neuronal activity indeed contributes to the stress-dependent development of depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that chemogenetic manipulation of cerebellar neurons (crus I PCs) during chronic stress alters depression-like behaviors.

claim: Iontophoretic injection of AAV-sSyn-GFP into the fastigial nucleus (FN) does not result in GFP-positive axonal projections in the VTA.
source: Upon injection into the FN, GFP-positive axonal projections were not observed in the VTA (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing no GFP-positive axons in the VTA after AAV injection into the FN, as shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Iontophoretic injection of AAV-sSyn-GFP into the interposed nucleus (IPN) results in clear GFP-positive axons in the red nucleus (RN).
source: Injection to the IPN clearly displayed GFP-positive axons in the red nucleus (RN), which is a well-known projection area from the cerebellum (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing GFP-positive axons in the RN after AAV injection into the IPN, as shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Iontophoretic injection of AAV-sSyn-GFP into the interposed nucleus (IPN) results in weak GFP-positive axonal projections in the contralateral dorsolateral anterior VTA.
source: However, there were only weak GFP-positive axonal projections from the IPN in the contralateral side of the dorsolateral anterior VTA and slightly stronger GFP signals in the dorsolateral posterior VTA (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing weak GFP-positive axons in the contralateral dorsolateral anterior VTA after AAV injection into the IPN, as shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Iontophoretic injection of AAV-sSyn-GFP into the interposed nucleus (IPN) results in slightly stronger GFP signals in the dorsolateral posterior VTA.
source: However, there were only weak GFP-positive axonal projections from the IPN in the contralateral side of the dorsolateral anterior VTA and slightly stronger GFP signals in the dorsolateral posterior VTA (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing slightly stronger GFP signals in the dorsolateral posterior VTA after AAV injection into the IPN, as shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Iontophoretic injection of AAV-sSyn-GFP into the dentate nucleus (DN) results in strong GFP-positive axons in the red nucleus (RN).
source: While the injection into the DN displayed strong GFP-positive axons in the RN, it also resulted in GFP signals mainly in the contralateral side of both the anterior and posterior VTA, and the signals were most abundant compared with the injection into the other two nuclei (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing strong GFP-positive axons in the RN after AAV injection into the DN, as shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Iontophoretic injection of AAV-sSyn-GFP into the dentate nucleus (DN) results in GFP signals mainly in the contralateral side of both the anterior and posterior VTA.
source: While the injection into the DN displayed strong GFP-positive axons in the RN, it also resulted in GFP signals mainly in the contralateral side of both the anterior and posterior VTA, and the signals were most abundant compared with the injection into the other two nuclei (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing GFP signals in the contralateral anterior and posterior VTA after AAV injection into the DN, as shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DCN neurons in the DN project mainly to the dorsolateral posterior VTA among all VTA regions.
source: Particularly, DCN neurons in the DN projected mainly to the dorsolateral posterior VTA among all VTA regions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing GFP signals are most abundant in the dorsolateral posterior VTA after AAV injection into the DN.

claim: The majority of DCN projections to the VTA are from the DN.
source: Thus, consistent with previous studies (Parker et al., 2014; Carta et al., 2019), our results showed the projection from the DN and the IPN, but not the FN, to the VTA, and also suggested that the majority of DCN projections to the VTA are from the DN.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing the most abundant GFP signals in the VTA after AAV injection into the DN compared to the IPN or FN, and is consistent with prior studies (Parker et al., 2014; Carta et al., 2019).

claim: Iontophoretic delivery of rAAV2-retro-CAG-sfGFP into the posterior VTA results in GFP signals in many DCN neurons of the DN.
source: When rAAV2-retro expressing GFP (rAAV2-retro-CAG-sfGFP) was iontophoretically delivered into the posterior VTA (Figure 3D), faint but clear GFP signals were detected in many DCN neurons of the DN, but in fewer neurons of the IPN (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing analysis showing GFP signals in many DCN neurons of the DN after rAAV2-retro injection into the posterior VTA, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Iontophoretic delivery of rAAV2-retro-CAG-sfGFP into the posterior VTA results in GFP signals in fewer neurons of the IPN compared to the DN.
source: When rAAV2-retro expressing GFP (rAAV2-retro-CAG-sfGFP) was iontophoretically delivered into the posterior VTA (Figure 3D), faint but clear GFP signals were detected in many DCN neurons of the DN, but in fewer neurons of the IPN (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from retrograde tracing analysis showing GFP signals in fewer neurons of the IPN compared to the DN after rAAV2-retro injection into the posterior VTA, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Injection of rAAV2-retro-CAG-iCre into the posterior VTA and AAV-sSyn-FLEX-GFP into the contralateral DCN results in strong GFP signals in many DCN neurons of the DN.
source: In another set of experiments, rAAV2-retro expressing Cre recombinase (rAAV2-retro-CAG-iCre) was injected into the posterior VTA, and AAV expressing GFP with a Cre-dependent genetic switch (AAV-sSyn-FLEX-GFP) was injected over a broad area of the contralateral DCN, including the DN and the IPN (Figure 3F). This combination of AAV injection resulted in strong GFP signals that were observed in many DCN neurons of the DN, but in only a few neurons of the IPN (Figure 3G, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from double injection retrograde tracing analysis showing strong GFP signals in many DCN neurons of the DN, as shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Injection of rAAV2-retro-CAG-iCre into the posterior VTA and AAV-sSyn-FLEX-GFP into the contralateral DCN results in GFP signals in only a few neurons of the IPN.
source: This combination of AAV injection resulted in strong GFP signals that were observed in many DCN neurons of the DN, but in only a few neurons of the IPN (Figure 3G, top).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from double injection retrograde tracing analysis showing GFP signals in only a few neurons of the IPN, as shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The small numbers of GFP-positive neurons in the IPN after double injection are not due to less efficient delivery of AAV into the IPN.
source: The small numbers of GFP-positive neurons in the IPN did not appear to be due to the less efficient delivery of AAV into the IPN, because tdTomato (tdT) signals derived from the simultaneous injection of AAV-sSyn-tdT was observed similarly in both the DN and IPN (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing similar tdTomato signals in both the DN and IPN, indicating efficient AAV delivery to both regions, as shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The VTA receives anatomical connectivity of DCN neurons mainly from the DN among all three DCN subregions.
source: These results of AAV-based tracing confirm that the VTA receives anatomical connectivity of DCN neurons mainly from the DN among all three DCN subregions, even though the VTA-projecting DCN neurons seemed to be only a part of all DCN neurons in the DN, as seen in the images of the cerebellum in Figure 3E and G.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data from multiple AAV-based tracing analyses showing the most abundant projections to the VTA from the DN compared to the IPN or FN, as shown in Figures 3E and 3G.

claim: VTA-projecting DCN neurons are only a part of all DCN neurons in the DN.
source: These results of AAV-based tracing confirm that the VTA receives anatomical connectivity of DCN neurons mainly from the DN among all three DCN subregions, even though the VTA-projecting DCN neurons seemed to be only a part of all DCN neurons in the DN, as seen in the images of the cerebellum in Figure 3E and G.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data from AAV-based tracing analyses showing that not all DCN neurons in the DN are labeled by retrograde tracing from the VTA, as seen in Figures 3E and 3G.

claim: Photostimulation of ChR2-expressing DCN axons triggers excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) in VTA neurons.
source: This photostimulation triggered EPSCs in VTA neurons (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing EPSCs in VTA neurons upon photostimulation of ChR2-expressing DCN axons, as shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Photostimulation-triggered EPSCs in VTA neurons are detected in only some of the VTA neurons (13 out of 54 neurons).
source: Although the photostimulation-triggered EPSCs were detected in only some of the VTA neurons (13 out of 54 neurons, Figure 4E), the responses were clearly and repeatedly observed upon photostimulation (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing EPSCs in 13 out of 54 VTA neurons, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The application of TTX inhibits photostimulation-triggered EPSCs in VTA neurons.
source: The application of TTX inhibited the photostimulation-triggered EPSCs, yet subsequent addition of 4-AP surmounted the TTX-dependent inhibition of EPSCs (Figure 4F; baseline – TTX: t(8) = 3.69, p = 0.006; TTX – TTX + 4-AP: t(8) = 2.63, p = 0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing TTX inhibits photostimulation-triggered EPSCs (p = 0.006), as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Subsequent addition of 4-AP surmounts the TTX-dependent inhibition of EPSCs in VTA neurons.
source: The application of TTX inhibited the photostimulation-triggered EPSCs, yet subsequent addition of 4-AP surmounted the TTX-dependent inhibition of EPSCs (Figure 4F; baseline – TTX: t(8) = 3.69, p = 0.006; TTX – TTX + 4-AP: t(8) = 2.63, p = 0.03).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing 4-AP surmounts TTX-dependent inhibition of EPSCs (p = 0.03), as shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The connections from the DCN to the VTA are monosynaptic.
source: Because 4-AP is considered to enhance depolarization of photostimulated ChR2-expressing axons and consequently induce neurotransmitter release even in the presence of TTX, the results indicate that the connections from the DCN to the VTA are monosynaptic.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that 4-AP can surmount TTX-dependent inhibition of EPSCs, which is a standard test for monosynaptic connections.

claim: Ih currents are not observed in most ZsGreen-positive neurons in the VTA of GAD2-IRES-Cre;Ai6 mice.
source: Indeed, Ih currents were not observed in most of ZsGreen-positive neurons whereas ZsGreen-negative neurons showed clear Ih currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; p = 0.0002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing Ih currents are not observed in most ZsGreen-positive neurons (p = 0.0002), as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ZsGreen-negative neurons in the VTA of GAD2-IRES-Cre;Ai6 mice show clear Ih currents.
source: Indeed, Ih currents were not observed in most of ZsGreen-positive neurons whereas ZsGreen-negative neurons showed clear Ih currents (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; p = 0.0002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing ZsGreen-negative neurons show clear Ih currents (p = 0.0002), as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Photostimulation-evoked EPSCs are recorded in both putative GABA and DA neurons in the VTA.
source: Photostimulation-evoked EPSCs were recorded in both putative GABA (Figure 4C) and DA neurons (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing EPSCs in both putative GABA and DA neurons, as shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: 5 neurons exhibiting EPSCs were identified as putative DA neurons and 7 neurons were identified as putative GABA neurons.
source: Except for one neuron that was unidentified due to the membrane seal being lost, 5 and 7 neurons exhibiting EPSCs were identified as putative DA and GABA neurons, respectively (Figure 4E), indicating the nonspecific projection of DCN neurons in the DN to both types of VTA neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing 5 putative DA neurons and 7 putative GABA neurons exhibiting EPSCs, as shown in Figure 4E.

claim: DCN neurons in the DN have nonspecific projection to both DA and GABA neurons in the VTA.
source: Except for one neuron that was unidentified due to the membrane seal being lost, 5 and 7 neurons exhibiting EPSCs were identified as putative DA and GABA neurons, respectively (Figure 4E), indicating the nonspecific projection of DCN neurons in the DN to both types of VTA neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing EPSCs in both putative DA and GABA neurons, indicating nonspecific projection.

claim: The peak amplitude of photostimulation-evoked EPSCs is equivalent between putative DA and GABA neurons.
source: The peak amplitude and time course of photostimulation-evoked EPSCs were equivalent between putative DA and GABA neurons (Figure 4G; peak amplitude: p = 0.21; time course: p = 0.66).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing no significant difference in peak amplitude between putative DA and GABA neurons (p = 0.21), as shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The time course of photostimulation-evoked EPSCs is equivalent between putative DA and GABA neurons.
source: The peak amplitude and time course of photostimulation-evoked EPSCs were equivalent between putative DA and GABA neurons (Figure 4G; peak amplitude: p = 0.21; time course: p = 0.66).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing no significant difference in time course between putative DA and GABA neurons (p = 0.66), as shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Structural synaptic connections of the DN-VTA circuit are verified using the mGRASPi technique.
source: Furthermore, structural synaptic connections of the DN-VTA circuit were verified through using the improved version of mammalian GFP reconstitution across synaptic partners (mGRASPi) technique, which enabled us to detect synaptic contacts using light microscopy (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using the mGRASPi technique to detect synaptic contacts, as referenced by Kim et al., 2011.

claim: Reconstituted mGRASP signals are detected between the button-like structures of anti-OLLAS-positive presynaptic DCN neuronal axons and a dT-positive postsynaptic VTA neuron.
source: As a result, reconstituted mGRASP signals were detected between the button-like structures of anti-OLLAS-positive presynaptic DCN neuronal axons and a dT-positive postsynaptic VTA neuron (Figure 4H), confirming DN-VTA synaptic connections.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mGRASPi analysis showing reconstituted mGRASP signals between DCN axons and VTA neurons, as shown in Figure 4H.

claim: DCN neurons in the DN make functional synaptic connections to putative DA and GABA neurons in the VTA.
source: These results of electrophysiological and mGRASP analyses demonstrated that DCN neurons in the DN make functional synaptic connections to putative DA and GABA neurons in the VTA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data from electrophysiological and mGRASP analyses showing functional and structural synaptic connections between DCN neurons and VTA neurons.

claim: Collateral axons of VTA-projecting DCN neurons with rosette shaped mossy fiber terminals (MFTs) are mainly present in crus I.
source: Whereas GFP-positive DCN neurons were in the DN and their axons were in the VTA (Figure 5A and B), screening of the entire cerebellar cortex demonstrated that their collateral axons with rosette shaped mossy fiber terminals (MFTs) were mainly present in crus I and were also present in crus II and the simplex lobe (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing collateral axons with MFTs are mainly present in crus I, as shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Collateral axons of VTA-projecting DCN neurons with rosette shaped mossy fiber terminals (MFTs) are also present in crus II and the simplex lobe.
source: Whereas GFP-positive DCN neurons were in the DN and their axons were in the VTA (Figure 5A and B), screening of the entire cerebellar cortex demonstrated that their collateral axons with rosette shaped mossy fiber terminals (MFTs) were mainly present in crus I and were also present in crus II and the simplex lobe (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing collateral axons with MFTs are also present in crus II and the simplex lobe, as shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GFP signals in collateral axons are specific to VTA-projecting DCN neurons.
source: These were specific GFP signals arising from VTA-projecting DCN neurons in spite of the sparse GFP signals in collateral axons, as there were no clear GFP signals detected in collateral axons without injection into the VTA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing no GFP signals in collateral axons without VTA injection, confirming specificity, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Crus I, II, and the simplex lobe receive feedback signals from DCN neurons in the DN that specifically project to the VTA.
source: These results indicate that crus I, II, and the simplex lobe receive feedback signals from DCN neurons in the DN, which specifically project to the VTA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data from neuronal tracing analysis showing collateral axons of VTA-projecting DCN neurons are present in crus I, II, and the simplex lobe.

claim: IPSCs are detected in VTA-projecting DCN neurons upon application of blue light stimuli to the DN in cerebellar sagittal slices.
source: For this purpose, we recorded optogenetically evoked inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) from VTA-projecting DCN neurons that were labeled by the retrograde tracer Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated cholera toxin B (CTB 647), after expressing ChR2 in crus I PCs (Figure 5D and E). IPSCs were detected upon the application of five trains of blue light stimuli to the DN in cerebellar sagittal slices (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing IPSCs in VTA-projecting DCN neurons upon photostimulation, as shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Optically induced IPSCs in VTA-projecting DCN neurons are completely abolished by treatment with bicuculline.
source: When the same slices were treated with 10 μM bicuculline, which is a GABA type A receptor antagonist, the optically induced IPSCs were completely abolished (Figure 5F and G; p = 0.001), confirming inhibitory synaptic transmission from PCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from whole-cell patch clamp recording showing optically induced IPSCs are completely abolished by bicuculline (p = 0.001), as shown in Figures 5F and 5G.

claim: Crus I PCs send synaptic inputs to DCN neurons in the DN that in turn project to the VTA.
source: These results verified the zonal organization of the corticonuclear and nucleocortical pathways in the VTA-associated cerebellar networks, and also identified that crus I PCs send synaptic inputs to DCN neurons in the DN that in turn project to the VTA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing IPSCs in VTA-projecting DCN neurons upon photostimulation of crus I PC axons, confirming synaptic connections.

claim: Chronic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons in the DN during restraint stress prevents stressed mice from showing depression-like behavior in the TST.
source: Whereas saline administration (RS-Gi-DN-Sal group) did not affect the immobility time prolonged by the RS in the TST and FST, CNO administration (RS-Gi-DN-CNO group) shortened the immobility time. As a result, the averaged immobility time in the RS-Gi-DN-CNO group was significantly shorter than that of the RS-Gi-DN-Sal group, and was similar to the CTR group in both the TST and FST (Figure 6B and C; RS-Gi-DN-Sal – RS-Gi-DN-CNO, TST: t(38) = –2.23, p = 0.03, FST: t(38) = –3.2, p = 0.002; CTR – RS-Gi-DN-CNO, TST: t(52) = 0.03, p = 0.98, FST: t(52) = 0.94, p = 0.35).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing chronic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons during RS significantly shortens immobility time in the TST compared to RS-Gi-DN-Sal (p = 0.03) and is similar to control (p = 0.98), as shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Chronic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons in the DN during restraint stress prevents stressed mice from showing depression-like behavior in the FST.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing chronic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons during RS significantly shortens immobility time in the FST compared to RS-Gi-DN-Sal (p = 0.002) and is similar to control (p = 0.35), as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: There are no differences in the distance traveled in the OFT among all groups (CTR, RS, RS-Gi-DN-Sal, RS-Gi-DN-CNO).
source: In the OFT, there were no differences in the distance traveled among all groups, demonstrating intact locomotor activity of the mice (Figure 6D; F(3,112) = 0.71, p = 0.55).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the open-field test showing no significant difference in distance traveled among the four groups (p = 0.55), as shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There is a significant correlation between TST and FST.
source: There was a significant correlation between TST and FST, but not between OFT and TST or FST (Table 1; TST – FST: r = 0.33, p < 0.001; TST – OFT: r = –0.12, p = 0.2; FST – OFT: r = 0.05, p = 0.06), indicating that the TST and FST measured share the behavioral phenotypes, likely the depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Pearson correlation coefficient analysis showing a significant correlation between TST and FST (r = 0.33, p < 0.001), as shown in Table 1.

claim: There is no significant correlation between OFT and TST.
source: There was a significant correlation between TST and FST, but not between OFT and TST or FST (Table 1; TST – FST: r = 0.33, p < 0.001; TST – OFT: r = –0.12, p = 0.2; FST – OFT: r = 0.05, p = 0.06), indicating that the TST and FST measured share the behavioral phenotypes, likely the depression-like behaviors.

claim: There is no significant correlation between FST and OFT.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Pearson correlation coefficient analysis showing no significant correlation between FST and OFT (r = 0.05, p = 0.06), as shown in Table 1.

claim: 2-week restraint stress application significantly decreases the time spent grooming in the sucrose splash test (SST).
source: The 2-week RS application significantly decreased the time spent grooming in the SST (Figure 6E; t(42) = –5.12, p < 0.001)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the sucrose splash test showing 2-week RS significantly decreases grooming time (p < 0.001), as shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 2-week restraint stress application significantly increases the latency to feed in the novelty suppressed feeding test (NSFT).
source: and significantly increased the latency to feed in the NSFT (Figure 6F; t(28) = 3.39, p = 0.001), without altering home cage food consumption (Figure 6G; t(28) = 1.14, p = 0.26).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the novelty suppressed feeding test showing 2-week RS significantly increases latency to feed (p = 0.001), as shown in Figure 6F.

claim: 2-week restraint stress application does not alter home cage food consumption.
source: and significantly increased the latency to feed in the NSFT (Figure 6F; t(28) = 3.39, p = 0.001), without altering home cage food consumption (Figure 6G; t(28) = 1.14, p = 0.26).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing 2-week RS does not significantly alter home cage food consumption (p = 0.26), as shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Chronic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons during restraint stress increases grooming time in the SST compared to the RS group.
source: The RS-Gi-DN-Sal group showed similar depression-like behaviors to the RS group in both the SST and NSFT (SST: t(39) = –0.84, p = 0.4; NSFT: t(29) = –0.626, p = 0.53). On the other hand, depression-like behaviors were reduced in the RS-Gi-DN-CNO group: mice in the RS-Gi-DN-CNO group spent significantly longer time in grooming in the SST, and took significantly less time to feed in the NSFT, compared with the RS group (Figure 6E and F; SST: t(40) = 2.8, p = 0.006; NSFT: t(30) = –2.12, p = 0.04).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the sucrose splash test showing chronic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons during RS significantly increases grooming time compared to RS alone (p = 0.006), as shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Chronic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons during restraint stress decreases latency to feed in the NSFT compared to the RS group.
source: On the other hand, depression-like behaviors were reduced in the RS-Gi-DN-CNO group: mice in the RS-Gi-DN-CNO group spent significantly longer time in grooming in the SST, and took significantly less time to feed in the NSFT, compared with the RS group (Figure 6E and F; SST: t(40) = 2.8, p = 0.006; NSFT: t(30) = –2.12, p = 0.04).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the novelty suppressed feeding test showing chronic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons during RS significantly decreases latency to feed compared to RS alone (p = 0.04), as shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Decreased activity of VTA-projecting DCN neurons in the DN inhibits depression-like behaviors.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that decreased activity of VTA-projecting DCN neurons in the DN, and possibly IPN, inhibits depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that chemogenetic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons during RS reduces depression-like behaviors in multiple tests (TST, FST, SST, NSFT).

claim: CNO administration itself without stereotaxic AAV injection does not affect immobility of control mice in the TST without RS application.
source: The CNO administration itself without stereotaxic AAV injection did not affect immobility of control mice in the TST and FST, because the CNO group showed similar immobility time to the CTR group, and significantly shorter immobility time than the RS group (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and C; CTR – Sal, TST: t(42) = 1.1, p = 0.27, FST: t(42) = 0.94, p = 0.35; CTR – CNO, TST: t(42) = 1.08, p = 0.28, FST: t(42) = 0.96, p = 0.34; RS – Sal, TST: t(42) = –2.71, p = 0.008, FST: t(42) = –2.6, p = 0.01; RS – CNO, TST: t(42) = –2.74, p = 0.008, FST: t(42) = –2.58, p = 0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing CNO administration without AAV injection does not significantly alter immobility time in the TST compared to control (p = 0.28), as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CNO administration itself without stereotaxic AAV injection does not affect immobility of control mice in the FST without RS application.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing CNO administration without AAV injection does not significantly alter immobility time in the FST compared to control (p = 0.34), as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Off-target effects of CNO have little or no impact on behavioral observation without RS application.
source: These results indicate that off-target effects of CNO, if any, have little or no impact on our behavioral observation without RS application.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing CNO administration without AAV injection does not significantly alter behavioral outcomes compared to control.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests showing the Gq-DN-CNO group has significantly longer immobility time in the FST compared to Gq-DN-Sal (p = 0.02).

claim: The increased immobility times of the Gq-DN-CNO groups in the TST and FST are not due to less locomotor activity.

evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the open-field test showing no significant difference in locomotor activity among groups (p = 0.11), as shown in Figure 7D.

source: Furthermore, when the OFT, TST, and FST were performed a week after the last CNO administration (Figure 7E), the results were similar to ones observed a few days after the last CNO administration: the immobility time in the Gq-DN-CNO group was significantly longer than the CTR and Gq-DN-Sal groups, but was similar to the RS group in both the TST and FST (Figure 7H and I; CTR – Gq-DN-CNO, TST: t(43) = 3.91, p < 0.001, FST: t(43) = 4.01, p < 0.001; Gq-DN-Sal – Gq-DN-CNO, TST: t(45) = 2.84, p = 0.006, FST: t(45) = 3.43, p < 0.001; RS – Gq-DN-CNO, TST: t(43) = –0.72, p = 0.47, FST: t(43) = 0.85, p = 0.4), whereas no difference was detected in the OFT (Figure 7J; F(3,85) = 0.43, p = 0.73). claim: Chronic activation of specific DCN neurons projecting from the DN to the VTA is triggered by chronic stress.
source: Taken together with the other results in this study, we conclude that chronic activation of specific DCN neurons projecting from the DN to the VTA is triggered by the chronic stress, and such activation itself proactively leads to the development of depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing increased c-Fos expression in the DN after chronic stress and behavioral data showing that manipulation of VTA-projecting DCN neurons alters depression-like behaviors.

claim: Chronic activation of specific DCN neurons projecting from the DN to the VTA proactively leads to the development of depression-like behaviors.
source: Taken together with the other results in this study, we conclude that chronic activation of specific DCN neurons projecting from the DN to the VTA is triggered by the chronic stress, and such activation itself proactively leads to the development of depression-like behaviors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that chronic activation of VTA-projecting DCN neurons alone is sufficient to trigger depression-like behaviors.

claim: The cerebellum directly contributes to the mechanism that develops depression-like behavior owing to stress, through the activation of a specific circuit composed of DCN neurons projecting to the VTA.
source: Our results demonstrated that chemogenetic excitation of crus I PCs suppressed the activation of DCN neurons in the DN and depression-like behaviors, both of which were triggered by the application of RS. As we identified neuronal networks of the DN connecting from crus I of the cerebellar cortex to the VTA, a brain region involved in the regulation of stress susceptibility (Fox and Lobo, 2019), we performed chemogenetic inhibition of VTA-projecting DCN neurons in the DN, and possibly the IPN. We found that the inhibition of these neurons during chronic RS also resulted in the suppression of depression-like behavior. These results indicate that the cerebellum directly contributes to the mechanism that develops depression-like behavior owing to stress, through the activation of a specific circuit composed of DCN neurons projecting to the VTA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that manipulation of cerebellar neurons (crus I PCs and VTA-projecting DCN neurons) during chronic stress alters depression-like behaviors.

claim: The activation of the neuronal circuit of VTA-projecting DCN neurons, which is regulated by crus I PCs, is a crucial determinant of the development of stress-mediated depression-like behaviors.
source: We thus conclude that the activation of the neuronal circuit of VTA-projecting DCN neurons, which is regulated by crus I PCs, is a crucial determinant of the development of stress-mediated depression-like behaviors (Figure 8), although the circuit may include not only a pathway to the VTA but also pathways to non-VTA regions via DCN collateral projections.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that manipulation of crus I PCs and VTA-projecting DCN neurons alters depression-like behaviors, as summarized in Figure 8.

claim: The cerebellum has been implicated in stress responses and stress-associated disorders.
source: Whereas the cerebellum has traditionally been considered to be important solely for motor coordination and learning, it became apparent that the cerebellum is also involved in higher cognitive functions (Rochefort et al., 2013; Hull, 2020; Wagner and Luo, 2020). One such non-motor cognitive function is reward-related processing (Carta et al., 2019; Medina, 2019; Hull, 2020; Sendhilnathan et al., 2020). Consistent with the common notion that reward circuitry regulates stress-driven behavioral changes or depressive symptoms (Nestler and Carlezon, 2006; Russo and Nestler, 2013; Pignatelli and Bonci, 2015; Fox and Lobo, 2019), many studies have demonstrated that abnormalities of the cerebellum are associated with stress responses or mental disorders, latter of which include major depressive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder that can be triggered or worsened by stress.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating the involvement of the cerebellum in stress responses and mental disorders.

claim: The cerebellum is affected by stress, as evident from alterations in function, structure, and molecular expression after exposure to stressful events.
source: The cerebellum is affected by stress, as is evident from the alterations in function, structure, and molecular expression that occur in the cerebellum after the exposure of animals or humans to stressful events (Gounko et al., 2013; Huguet et al., 2017; Bambico et al., 2018; Moreno-Rius, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Gounko et al., 2013; Huguet et al., 2017; Bambico et al., 2018; Moreno-Rius, 2019) demonstrating alterations in the cerebellum after stress exposure.

claim: Alterations of the cerebellum, such as decreased volume, abnormal neuronal activity, and disrupted cortical connectivity, have been observed in patients with major depressive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.
source: Alterations of the cerebellum, such as decreased volume, abnormal neuronal activity, and disrupted cortical connectivity, have also been observed in patients with major depressive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, and such alterations are often correlated with symptoms of these disorders (De Bellis and Kuchibhatla, 2006; Alalade et al., 2011; Baldaçara et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2012; Guo et al., 2013; Phillips et al., 2015; Córdova-palomera, 2016; Xu et al., 2017; Depping et al., 2018; Moreno-Rius, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies demonstrating cerebellar alterations in patients with major depressive disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder.

claim: The VTA is the origin of dopaminergic neurons projecting to other reward-related brain regions.
source: The VTA is the origin of dopaminergic neurons projecting to other reward-related brain regions, so that it is considered as a central component of reward circuitry.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the VTA and its role in reward circuitry.

claim: The VTA is involved in the regulation of stress susceptibility.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a prior study (Fox and Lobo, 2019) demonstrating the VTA's role in stress susceptibility.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Chaudhury et al., 2013; Tye et al., 2013; Friedman et al., 2014; Isingrini et al., 2016) demonstrating that stressful events alter VTA DA neuron activities.
